questions.stem: A phylogenetic tree of primates has several points where one line splits into two. What does each of these splitting points stand for?
options: A common ancestor from which the branches diverged
A species that is alive today at the tip of a branch
A mass extinction that ended every branch at that point
A fossil that has been dated using radiocarbon dating
questions.explanation: Each node represents the most recent common ancestor of the groups that branch from it. The tips of the branches represent living or extinct groups being compared.

questions.stem: In a phylogenetic tree, humans and chimpanzees share a more recent node than either does with gorillas. What does this show?
options: Gorillas are more closely related to humans than chimpanzees are to humans
Humans, chimpanzees and gorillas all diverged from one another at the same time
They share a more recent common ancestor than either does with gorillas
Humans evolved from chimpanzees, which had earlier evolved directly from gorillas
questions.explanation: A more recent shared node means a more recent common ancestor and closer relationship. The tree does not show humans descending from living chimpanzees; both are descended from a shared ancestor.

questions.stem: What is the main type of evidence now used to build phylogenetic trees of living primates?
options: Comparisons of the climates they live in
Comparisons of the foods they prefer to eat
Comparisons of DNA and protein sequences
Comparisons of body size and lifespan
questions.explanation: Comparative biochemistry, especially DNA sequences, gives large amounts of objective data about relationships, and is combined with anatomical and fossil evidence. Diet and climate reflect the environment rather than ancestry.

questions.stem: A phylogenetic tree is revised after new DNA sequence data show that two groups once thought distant are each other's closest relatives. What does this illustrate about scientific models?
options: Models are revised only when new fossils are discovered
Models are refined when new evidence becomes available
Models are fixed once they have been published in a journal
Models based on DNA are always wrong and must be replaced
questions.explanation: Phylogenetic trees are hypotheses about relationships. As comparative biochemistry and bioinformatics produce new data, trees are tested and refined, which is how science improves its models.

questions.stem: A hominin dies near a lake. Which circumstances would give its remains the best chance of becoming a fossil?
options: Being washed onto rocks and broken up by waves for years
Rapid burial in fine lake sediment with little oxygen
Lying exposed on the shore where scavengers are active
Slow decay on the surface in warm, well-aired conditions
questions.explanation: Fossils form most often when remains are buried quickly, protecting them from scavengers, oxygen and decomposers, and when there are hard parts such as bones and teeth that can be mineralised.

questions.stem: Why is the fossil record described as incomplete?
options: Fossils form only from organisms that lived in the last ten thousand years
Every organism fossilises, but most fossils are too small to be studied
Scientists have chosen to study only fossils of vertebrate animals
Few organisms fossilise, and many fossils are destroyed or never found
questions.explanation: Fossilisation needs special conditions, so most organisms leave no trace. Fossils can later be destroyed by erosion or rock movement, and many remain buried or in inaccessible places.

questions.stem: Early hominins lived mainly in grassland and woodland. Why might their fossils be under-represented compared with animals that lived in lakes and swamps?
options: Remains on dry land are less likely to be buried quickly in sediment
Hominin bones were too dense to be preserved by mineral replacement
Hominins lived too recently for any of their remains to fossilise
Hominin remains are always destroyed by volcanic eruptions
questions.explanation: Lakes, rivers and swamps deposit sediment that can bury remains rapidly. On dry land, bodies are more often scavenged, scattered and decomposed before burial, so fewer fossils form.

questions.stem: Many important hominin fossils have been found in the East African Rift Valley. Which factor best explains why fossils are found there more readily than in many other places?
options: Faulting and erosion have exposed old sedimentary layers at the surface
Early hominins lived only in this valley and nowhere else in Africa at any time
The climate of the valley prevents all decay, so every organism there fossilised
Fossils in the valley are younger, so they have not yet been destroyed by erosion
questions.explanation: Accessibility affects the fossil record. Faulting and erosion in the Rift Valley expose ancient sediment layers, many interbedded with volcanic ash that can be dated. Elsewhere, fossils may exist but remain deeply buried.

questions.stem: Fossilised footprints made by early hominins have been found in hardened volcanic ash. What type of fossil are they?
options: A trace fossil
A body fossil
An index fossil
A cast of a bone
questions.explanation: Trace fossils preserve evidence of activity, such as footprints, rather than parts of the body itself. Footprints can show how an animal walked, which is useful evidence of bipedalism.

questions.stem: Which principle underlies dating by stratigraphy?
options: In undisturbed rock layers, lower layers are older than higher layers
In undisturbed rock layers, higher layers are older than lower layers
All rock layers in one area were deposited at exactly the same time
Rock layers can be dated in years by measuring their thickness alone
questions.explanation: The law of superposition states that sedimentary layers are laid down in order, with the oldest at the bottom. This gives the relative ages of fossils in different layers, but not their ages in years.

questions.stem: Stratigraphy and index fossils are relative dating methods. What can they not provide?
options: The order in which fossils were deposited
Whether one fossil is older than another
A link between layers at different sites
An age for the fossil in years
questions.explanation: Relative dating tells us whether a fossil is older or younger than another but does not give a numerical age. Absolute dating methods are needed for that.

questions.stem: A geologist wants fossils that will help match rock layers of the same age at distant sites. Which species would be the best choice?
options: One with soft body parts that rarely left any remains
One that was widespread, abundant and existed only briefly
One that was rare, lived in one place and existed for a long time
One that is still alive today and has changed very little
questions.explanation: An index fossil comes from a species that was common and geographically widespread but lasted only a short time, so its presence identifies a narrow time range in rock layers in different places.

questions.stem: In a cliff, fossil X is found in layer 2 and fossil Y in layer 5, counting up from the bottom. Earth movements have since folded the layers so that part of the sequence is overturned. What can be concluded?
options: Fossil Y must be older than fossil X, because folding always reverses every layer
Both fossils must be the same age, because folding mixes all the layers together
Lower layers may not be older here, so the order must be checked
Fossil X must be older than fossil Y, because it is lower down in the cliff
questions.explanation: Stratigraphy assumes layers are undisturbed. Folding, faulting and erosion can overturn or remove layers, so other evidence, such as index fossils or absolute dating, is needed to confirm their order.

questions.stem: Fossils of a particular extinct pig species, known to have lived only during a narrow time span, are found in the same layer as a hominin fossil at a new site. How does this help?
options: The pig fossils give an exact age in years for the hominin fossil
The pig fossils show that the hominin evolved directly from pigs
The pig fossils can be radiocarbon dated to millions of years old
They act as index fossils, indicating the age range of the layer
questions.explanation: Fossils of short-lived, widespread species can be used to correlate layers between sites and estimate their age range. This is relative dating, and an absolute method would be needed for a numerical age.

questions.stem: What is absolute dating?
options: Finding a sample's age in years, usually from radioactive decay
Placing fossils in order from oldest to youngest using rock layers
Comparing a fossil's shape with that of a living species
Estimating age from how deeply a fossil is buried
questions.explanation: Absolute (radiometric) dating uses the known rate of decay of radioactive isotopes to calculate an age in years. Placing fossils in order using rock layers is relative dating.

questions.stem: A layer of volcanic ash at a fossil site has been dated at about 3.6 million years old. Which method was most likely used?
options: Radiocarbon dating
Stratigraphy
Index fossils
Potassium-argon dating
questions.explanation: Potassium-argon dating suits volcanic rock and can date material millions of years old. Radiocarbon dating works only up to about 50,000 years, and stratigraphy and index fossils give relative, not numerical, ages.

questions.stem: Radiocarbon dating measures the decay of carbon-14. What kind of sample can it date?
options: Organic remains such as bone, up to about 50,000 years old
Volcanic rock layers from millions of years ago, such as basalt
Any rock, as long as it contains fossils of animals
Stone tools made from rock with no carbon in them
questions.explanation: Carbon-14 is taken in by living things and decays after death. With a half-life of about 5730 years, too little remains after about 50,000 years to measure, so the method suits younger organic material.

questions.stem: A sample of charcoal from a hearth contains one-quarter of the carbon-14 it would have had when the wood was alive. Using a half-life of 5730 years, about how old is it?
options: 1432 years
11,460 years
5730 years
22,920 years
questions.explanation: One-quarter remaining means two half-lives have passed: 1 to 1/2 to 1/4. Two half-lives is 2 × 5730 = 11,460 years. One half-life would leave one-half, and four would leave one-sixteenth.

questions.stem: Why is potassium-argon dating used to date layers of volcanic rock rather than fossils themselves?
options: Volcanic rock contains carbon-14, which is converted into argon over thousands of years
Volcanic rock contains potassium-40, and argon from its decay builds up after cooling
Potassium-40 is found only in bone, so the rock around the fossil must be dated first
Argon is absorbed by living things, so fossils contain too much of it to give a result
questions.explanation: When volcanic rock forms, argon gas escapes; afterwards, argon-40 from the decay of potassium-40 is trapped in the rock. Measuring the ratio dates when the rock formed, so fossils between dated layers can be given an age range.

questions.stem: A hominin fossil lies in sediment between two volcanic ash layers. Potassium-argon dating gives the lower ash 2.1 million years and the upper ash 1.8 million years. What can be concluded about the fossil?
options: It is younger than 1.8 million years, above both layers
It is between about 1.8 and 2.1 million years old
It is exactly 1.95 million years old, halfway between
It is older than 2.1 million years, below both layers
questions.explanation: Combining stratigraphy with absolute dating brackets the fossil: it is younger than the layer beneath it and older than the layer above it. There is no basis for choosing the exact midpoint.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly gives a limitation of each absolute dating method?
options: Radiocarbon dating gives only relative ages; potassium-argon gives exact ages
Radiocarbon cannot date old samples; potassium-argon needs volcanic rock
Radiocarbon dating needs volcanic rock; potassium-argon cannot date old samples
Radiocarbon dating can date only stone; potassium-argon can date only bone
questions.explanation: Carbon-14's short half-life limits radiocarbon dating to organic remains less than about 50,000 years old. Potassium-argon dating suits much older material but only works on volcanic rocks, so sites without volcanic layers cannot be dated this way.

questions.stem: A team finds a hominin skull thought to be about 1.5 million years old in cave sediments with no volcanic rock. Why would neither radiocarbon nor potassium-argon dating be suitable?
options: The skull is too young for carbon-14, and the cave rock contains too much potassium
Carbon-14 cannot be used on bone, and potassium-argon cannot be used in Africa
Both methods can date only stone tools, not skulls or the sediment around them
It is far too old for carbon-14, and there is no volcanic rock to date
questions.explanation: After 1.5 million years virtually no carbon-14 would remain, and potassium-argon requires volcanic rock. Researchers would need other methods, such as index fossils or other dating techniques suited to cave deposits.

questions.stem: What are homologous structures, and what do they suggest?
options: Structures that have lost their function, showing species are not related
Structures found only in fossils, showing species did not change over time
Same basic plan, different functions; they suggest a common ancestor
Structures with similar functions but different origins, suggesting a common ancestor
questions.explanation: Homologous structures, such as the forelimb bones of humans, whales and bats, share a basic arrangement inherited from a common ancestor, even though they are now used differently. Similar functions from different origins describe analogous structures.

questions.stem: Which human structure is usually described as vestigial, and so is cited as evidence of evolution?
options: The femur (thigh bone)
The sternum (breastbone)
The scapula (shoulder blade)
The coccyx (tailbone)
questions.explanation: The coccyx is a small set of fused vertebrae that corresponds to the tail of other primates and mammals. Vestigial structures are reduced remnants of structures that were functional in ancestors.

questions.stem: The amino acid sequence of cytochrome c is identical in humans and chimpanzees, but differs at more positions between humans and less closely related animals. What does this suggest?
options: Cytochrome c has never mutated in any species since it first evolved
Humans and chimpanzees eat the same diet, so their proteins are alike
Species with more differences in a protein are the more recently evolved
More similar sequences indicate a more recent common ancestor
questions.explanation: Mutations accumulate in separated lineages over time, so the fewer differences there are between two species' sequences, the more recently they shared an ancestor. Diet does not determine protein sequence.

questions.stem: Why do DNA sequence comparisons often give more information about relatedness than protein sequence comparisons?
options: DNA shows changes such as silent mutations that do not alter the protein
DNA is found only in the closely related species that are being compared
DNA sequences never change, so they show the original ancestral form
DNA comparisons can be made without any knowledge of the base sequence
questions.explanation: Because the genetic code is degenerate, some mutations change the DNA but not the amino acid sequence. DNA comparisons detect these, and also include non-coding regions, giving finer detail.

questions.stem: The idea of a molecular clock is used to estimate when two species diverged. What assumption does it rely on?
options: Mutations stop once two species are no longer able to interbreed
Mutations in a DNA sequence build up at a fairly steady rate
Mutations in DNA occur only when a species moves to a new environment
Mutations accumulate faster in species that are more closely related
questions.explanation: If differences build up at a fairly steady rate, the number of differences between two species can be converted into time since divergence, calibrated using dated fossils. The rate can vary between genes and lineages, which is a limitation.

questions.stem: Mitochondrial DNA is often used to study human evolution and migration. Which feature makes it useful?
options: It is inherited only from the father and changes very slowly
It is found in the nucleus, so it is easy to separate out
It is identical in every living person, so it shows no change
It is inherited only from the mother and does not recombine
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial DNA passes from mother to child without being shuffled by recombination, so changes reflect mutations in the maternal line. Its relatively fast mutation rate and many copies per cell are also useful.

questions.stem: Scientists sequenced Neanderthal DNA from fossil bones and compared it with modern human genomes. People of non-African descent carry a small percentage of DNA that matches Neanderthal sequences. What is the best explanation?
options: The match is due to the same mutations arising independently in both groups
Modern humans inherited the DNA by eating Neanderthal remains thousands of years ago
Neanderthals and modern humans interbred after humans left Africa
Neanderthals evolved from modern humans who left Africa and later returned there
questions.explanation: The shared DNA is best explained by gene flow: modern humans and Neanderthals interbred where their ranges overlapped outside Africa. This evidence, from DNA sequencing and bioinformatics, has refined models of human evolution.

questions.stem: Researchers comparing the DNA of primate species often begin with PCR. Which job does this technique perform for them?
options: To make many copies of a chosen section of DNA
To separate DNA fragments according to their size
To cut DNA at specific sequences of bases
To insert a gene into a bacterial plasmid
questions.explanation: PCR amplifies a chosen DNA sequence, producing millions of copies from a tiny starting amount. This is valuable for fossils and other samples with very little DNA. Separating fragments by size is gel electrophoresis.

questions.stem: What happens in the three main steps of each PCR cycle?
options: Primers are heated to separate them, strands bind together, and ligase joins the fragments
DNA is cut by enzymes, fragments move through a gel, and bands are stained
DNA is transcribed into mRNA, translated into protein, and the protein is copied
Heat separates strands, primers bind on cooling, then polymerase builds new strands
questions.explanation: Heating to about 95 °C separates the strands, cooling lets primers attach to each side of the target, and heat-tolerant DNA polymerase extends the primers to make new strands. Repeating the cycle doubles the target each time.

questions.stem: Starting with one double-stranded copy of a DNA sequence, how many copies would ideally be present after 10 cycles of PCR?
questions.explanation: Each cycle doubles the number of copies, so after n cycles there are 2 to the power n copies. After 10 cycles that is 1024. The value 512 is the number after 9 cycles.

questions.stem: DNA samples from three primates are loaded into a gel and a current is applied. Why do the fragments move towards the positive electrode, and which go furthest?
options: DNA is positively charged; the largest fragments travel furthest
DNA is negatively charged; the largest fragments travel furthest
DNA is positively charged; the smallest fragments travel furthest
DNA is negatively charged; the smallest fragments travel furthest
questions.explanation: The phosphate groups give DNA a negative charge, so it is attracted to the positive electrode. The gel acts as a sieve, so short fragments move through it more easily and travel further than long ones.

questions.stem: DNA from three species is cut with the same restriction enzyme and run on a gel. Species A and B share most band positions, while species C shares few with either. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: C has less DNA than A and B, so it must have evolved more recently
A and B are more closely related to each other than either is to C
C is the common ancestor from which A and B both evolved recently
A and B are the same species, because some of their bands match
questions.explanation: Similar band patterns indicate similar DNA sequences at the enzyme's cutting sites, which suggests closer relationship. Shared bands do not show that species are identical, and a living species cannot be the ancestor of other living species.

questions.stem: Which description of the field of bioinformatics is accurate?
options: Using microscopes to compare the shapes of fossil bones from different rock layers
Using radioactive isotopes to work out the absolute age of fossil remains
Using selective breeding to produce organisms with useful combinations of traits
Using computers to store, search and compare data such as DNA sequences
questions.explanation: Bioinformatics combines biology, computing and statistics. Software aligns and compares sequences from databases, allowing relationships among many species to be analysed quickly.

questions.stem: How have DNA sequencing and bioinformatics together changed the study of human evolution?
options: Sequencing has shown that all great apes have identical genomes with no differences at all
Genomes can be compared rapidly, revealing relationships and gene flow
DNA can now be recovered from any fossil, however old, so dating methods are no longer needed
Fossils are no longer studied, because DNA gives complete information about every ancestor
questions.explanation: Fast sequencing produces enormous amounts of data, and bioinformatics allows it to be compared, revealing details such as interbreeding between groups. DNA rarely survives beyond a few hundred thousand years, so fossils and dating remain essential.

questions.stem: Ancient DNA recovered from a fossil bone is present in very small amounts and is badly fragmented. Which technique would scientists use first so that there is enough DNA to analyse?
options: Radiocarbon dating, to increase the amount of DNA
Stratigraphy, to separate the DNA from the bone
PCR, to amplify the DNA fragments of interest
Gel electrophoresis, to make more copies of DNA
questions.explanation: PCR makes many copies of targeted DNA sequences from tiny samples, allowing them to be sequenced. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA by size but does not copy it.
